catalog_quote: Word-level stress. In morphologically simplex words, primary stress falls predictably on the second mora. This means that when the first syllable of a word contains a long vowel, primary stress is word-initial, as in (9a). Otherwise, as in (9b), primary stress falls on the second syllable. (9) a. paa'a [ˈpʰaːʔa] 'water' b. pa'a [pʰaˈʔa] 'high'. In Mono Lake Northern Paiute, stress is cued by pitch and vowel length. Vowels in stressed syllables are higher in pitch and have longer durations than equivalent vowels in unstressed syllables. ... Any vowel following a primary stressed syllable can be devoiced, though typically word-final vowels are affected. [p. 241, preceding paragraph:] And, as Nichols observes (p. 42), the sixth vowel usually counts only as a single mora, which means that, when it occurs in a word-initial syllable, primary word stress falls on the second syllable, as in (8). [Snapp, Anderson & Anderson 1982: 6] Most second-syllable vowels of a word are long. The only exception is when the first-syllable vowel is long. Some suffixes contain a long vowel as well. Length is written only when not on the second syllable. ... The primary word stress and highest pitch occur on the long vowel, except on a very few words where the length is on the first syllable but the stress on the second. The lowest pitch immediately follows the highest pitch. Secondary stress pitches occur on every even syllable after the primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the second mora of the word: on the first syllable if it contains a long vowel (bimoraic), otherwise on the second syllable. This is the Numic second-mora system; at the moraic level it is fixed, at the syllabic level it depends on the weight of the initial syllable. The Fort McDermitt sketch (Snapp et al. 1982) describes the same thing from the other side: the second-syllable vowel is long unless the first is, and primary stress plus highest pitch sit on that long vowel. Stress is cued by higher pitch and longer duration; vowels after the primary stress may devoice.
new_statements.secondary_stress: JIPA 2012 says nothing about secondary stress. Snapp et al. 1982: 6: 'Secondary stress pitches occur on every even syllable after the primary stress' (i.e. alternating rhythm rightward from the primary).
new_statements.exceptions: JIPA restricts the rule to morphologically simplex words (no statement for complex words). The Numic 'sixth vowel' /e/ (Mono Lake only) counts as a single mora even when realized as a diphthong, so an initial /e/ syllable gets second-syllable stress (JIPA p. 241 citing Nichols 1974: 42). Snapp et al. 1982: 6 note 'a very few words where the length is on the first syllable but the stress on the second'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (JIPA section is titled 'Word-level stress'; examples are citation forms). Snapp et al. 1982: 7 separately describe sentence stress: up to three per clause, falling on the last word of a phrase on the syllable bearing primary word stress, with isochronous spacing of stress groups.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement is from the JIPA Illustration of the Mono Lake variety (southernmost, California; falls under Glottolog's South Northern Paiute dialect sout2967). The corroborating sketch (Snapp, Anderson & Anderson 1982) describes the Fort McDermitt (Nevada, north of the Humboldt) dialect, i.e. the northern group (North Northern Paiute nort1551); both agree on second-mora stress. Kataoka 2010 (silent on placement) concerns Southern Nevada Northern Paiute. Glottolog's listing of Loether 2003 (Owens Valley Paiute) under nort2954 is an identity mismatch: that variety is Mono (mono1275), which Snapp et al. 1982 p. 1 explicitly exclude.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Babel, Houser & Toosarvandani 2012 statement (second mora: second syllable, or first if its vowel is long); adds secondary stress on every even syllable after the primary, a few lexical exceptions, and sentence-stress placement. Describes the Fort McDermitt (Nevada) dialect, whereas Babel et al. describe Mono Lake. The listed SIL open_url (front-matter PDF) and the SIL archive landing page both returned 404 in two attempts; archive.org holds no full copy of the volume, only the Rosetta Project excerpts of this sketch, which were already held by the project from the earlier reading.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (with the highest pitch) falls on the long vowel of the word; since the second-syllable vowel is long by default, stress is on the second syllable unless the first-syllable vowel is long, in which case it is initial (i.e. on the second mora). Examples: /nana/ [nana·] 'man', /naana/ [na·na] 'men', /tɨnijui/ [tɨni·jui] 'teach', /na-tɨnijui/ [natɨ·nijui] 'learn'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress pitches occur on every even syllable after the primary stress (p. 6). Sentence stress falls on the last word of the phrase, on the syllable with primary word stress; up to three sentence stresses per clause, one on the verb, one on a topicalized phrase (p. 7).
new_statements.exceptions: A very few words have length on the first syllable but stress on the second (p. 6).
new_statements.identity_note: The Northern Paiute sketch in Langacker 1982 (Snapp, Anderson & Anderson) describes the dialect of the Fort McDermitt reservation, Nevada (introduction, p. 1); the existing statement from Babel et al. 2012 describes Mono Lake Northern Paiute, the southernmost variety. Both authors treat all dialects from Lee Vining to Fort Hall as mutually intelligible and the stress rule is stated identically.
